title: Smallpox inoculation practised across Asia, Africa and the Ottoman world
summary: Long before vaccination, people in China, parts of Africa and the Ottoman Empire deliberately gave healthy people a mild smallpox infection to protect them. European and colonial American physicians learned the practice from these traditions.
explanation:
Inoculation, later called variolation, introduced material from a smallpox sore or scab into a healthy person. The resulting illness was usually milder than naturally caught smallpox and left lifelong immunity, although some inoculated people died and they could infect others.

The earliest written discussion of the practice is in a Chinese book first published in 1549, which describes blowing powdered scab material into the nose. A Chinese tradition dates its invention to 1567–1572; a much-repeated claim that it began around 1000 CE rests on little documentation. Claims of ancient origins in India are not supported by Sanskrit medical texts, and an eighteenth-century report of Indian practice is doubtful.

In Constantinople, physicians reported to the Royal Society in London in 1714 and 1716 that inoculation had been introduced by a Greek woman around 1660 and had spread after an epidemic in 1700. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu had her son inoculated there and in 1721 had her daughter inoculated in London. In the same year, Onesimus, an enslaved African man, described inoculation in his homeland to the Boston minister Cotton Mather. The origins of the practice remain obscure, and it may be much older than any surviving record.

date.basis: From the earliest surviving written discussion (a Chinese book first published in 1549) to its reports reaching Britain and New England by 1721. The practice may be considerably older.

title: Boston's inoculation controversy and its numbers
summary: During Boston's 1721 smallpox epidemic, Zabdiel Boylston inoculated 282 people on the advice of Cotton Mather, who had learned of the practice from Onesimus. Boylston's counts suggested far lower mortality among the inoculated.
explanation:
When smallpox reached Boston in 1721, the minister Cotton Mather urged physicians to try inoculation. He had read reports from Constantinople in the Royal Society's journal and had heard about the practice from Onesimus, an African man he enslaved. Only one physician, Zabdiel Boylston, agreed.

The experiment provoked fury: inoculated people could spread smallpox, and critics mocked the practice for having been learned from Africans. Someone threw an explosive device through Mather's window. Boylston nonetheless kept records. Among 282 people he inoculated, 6 died (about 2%); among 5,759 residents who caught smallpox naturally and were not inoculated, 884 died (about 15%).

These numbers, together with comparable English figures collected by James Jurin, were among the earliest attempts to judge a medical practice by counting outcomes in comparable groups.

title: Jenner tests cowpox as protection against smallpox
summary: On 14 May 1796 Edward Jenner inoculated eight-year-old James Phipps with material from a milkmaid's cowpox sore, then showed the boy did not react to smallpox. His 1798 publication launched vaccination.
explanation:
Country people had long observed that milkmaids who caught cowpox, a mild disease, seemed to escape smallpox. Edward Jenner, a physician in Berkeley, Gloucestershire, set out to test the idea. On 14 May 1796 he took material from a cowpox lesion on the hand of a milkmaid, Sarah Nelmes, and inoculated James Phipps, the son of his gardener. Six weeks later he inoculated the boy with smallpox material, and no disease followed.

Jenner gathered further cases and published An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae in 1798. Vaccination, from the Latin for cow, was safer than variolation because it did not produce smallpox and could not spread it. Within a few years it was being carried around the world.

Jenner was not the first to try cowpox deliberately: in 1774 the Dorset farmer Benjamin Jesty had inoculated his wife and two sons with cowpox during a smallpox outbreak. Jenner's contribution was systematic testing and publication.

title: Lind compares six remedies for scurvy at sea
summary: On 20 May 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury, the naval surgeon James Lind gave twelve sailors with scurvy one of six treatments in pairs. The two given oranges and lemons recovered fastest.
explanation:
Scurvy killed huge numbers of sailors on long voyages. James Lind chose twelve men whose cases were as similar as he could find, kept them in the same part of the ship on the same diet, and assigned pairs to cider, elixir of vitriol, vinegar, sea water, oranges and lemons, or a purgative paste. Within six days one of the men given citrus was fit for duty, and the other was well enough to nurse the rest.

This deliberate comparison of treatments under similar conditions is one of the best-known early examples of a controlled clinical trial. Yet Lind's 1753 Treatise of the Scurvy did not single out citrus as a decisive cure, and its recommendations had little immediate impact. The Royal Navy did not issue citrus juice routinely until 1795, more than four decades later.

title: The Chamberlens' secret obstetric forceps
summary: Around 1600 a London family of surgeons and midwives, the Chamberlens, devised forceps that could deliver a living baby from an obstructed labour. They kept the design secret for over a century.
explanation:
Before forceps, an obstructed labour often ended with instruments that saved the mother only by destroying the child, or with the death of both. The Chamberlens, a Huguenot family settled in England, devised curved blades that could be applied separately around the baby's head and then joined, allowing a live birth.

The invention was probably made by Peter Chamberlen the elder and promoted by his nephew, Dr Peter Chamberlen. The family guarded it closely, working under blankets so that no one could see the instrument, and passed the secret down through four or five generations. Similar instruments were developed independently in Flanders and Holland, and forceps only became widely known in the early eighteenth century.

The original instruments were found in 1813 hidden at Woodham Mortimer Hall in Essex.

date.basis: The invention cannot be dated precisely; it is attributed to the late 16th or early 17th century. Forceps became widely known only in the early 18th century.

title: Stadaconan healers cure Cartier's crew of scurvy
summary: In the winter of 1535–36 Jacques Cartier's crew was dying of scurvy at Stadacona. Domagaya, son of the Stadaconan chief, showed them a remedy called annedda, an infusion of evergreen bark and leaves, prepared by two local women.
explanation:
Cartier's ships were frozen in near the village of Stadacona, on the site of present-day Quebec City, from November 1535. By February 1536 only 10 of his 110 men were in good health, and 25 eventually died. Cartier tried to hide his crew's weakness from the local people.

He learned of the cure from Domagaya, whom he had taken to France the year before. At Cartier's request, Domagaya had two women prepare the remedy from the bark and foliage of a conifer the Stadaconans called annedda, probably eastern white cedar. The sick recovered quickly.

The knowledge did not stay with the Europeans. When Roberval's party wintered near the same place in 1542, about 50 of 200 men died of scurvy, apparently without using the remedy.

title: Nahua physicians record Indigenous plant medicine
summary: In 1552, at the Colegio de Santa Cruz in Tlatelolco, the Nahua physician Martín de la Cruz composed an illustrated herbal of Indigenous medicine, translated into Latin by Juan Badiano. It is the earliest surviving illustrated work on Nahua medicine and botany.
explanation:
The Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco was founded to educate sons of the Nahua nobility. Martín de la Cruz, the college's Indigenous physician, set down remedies from Nahua medical knowledge, and Juan Badiano, a Nahua Latin teacher, translated them. The book, made for Francisco de Mendoza, son of the viceroy of New Spain, who sent it to Spain, contains some 185 painted plant illustrations alongside remedies.

The manuscript is unusual among sixteenth-century records of the Americas because it was written and translated by Indigenous authors rather than by European observers. Its blend of Nahua knowledge and European herbal form reflects the colonial setting in which it was made; the Nahuatl original has not survived.

The Latin manuscript spent nearly four centuries in European libraries, including the Vatican, where it was rediscovered in 1929. In 1990 Pope John Paul II returned it to Mexico, where it is held by the National Institute of Anthropology and History.

title: Cinchona bark enters medicine against fevers
summary: In the 1630s Jesuit missionaries in the Viceroyalty of Peru began using the bark of the Andean cinchona tree to treat intermittent fevers, and sent it to Europe. Its active ingredient, quinine, was isolated in Paris in 1820.
explanation:
The bark of cinchona trees, from the eastern slopes of the Andes, became known in Europe as 'Jesuits' bark' or 'Peruvian bark'. Jesuit missionaries were using it against fevers by about 1630, and shipments reached Europe in the following years, where it became the first effective treatment for malaria.

Popular stories credit its discovery to a feverish Indigenous man who drank water steeped with fallen cinchona, or to the cure of a Spanish countess. These are legends. Whether Andean peoples used the bark against fevers before European contact is uncertain.

Almost two centuries later, in 1820, the French pharmacists Pierre-Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Caventou isolated quinine from the bark. Purified quinine replaced the bark and allowed reliable dosing, decades before the malaria parasite itself was identified.

title: Vesalius's Fabrica rebuilds anatomy on dissection
summary: In 1543 Andreas Vesalius, professor at Padua, published De humani corporis fabrica in Basel: seven books of human anatomy based on his own dissections, with detailed woodcut illustrations that corrected many errors inherited from Galen.
explanation:
Vesalius, a young professor of anatomy and surgery at the University of Padua, insisted that reliable knowledge of the body must come from examining cadavers rather than from ancient texts. He spent much of 1542 dissecting and working with artists to prepare the woodcuts, then took the work to the printer Johannes Oporinus in Basel, where it appeared in 1543.

The Fabrica was the first profusely illustrated anatomy book. By comparing the human body with Galen's descriptions, many of them based on animal dissection, Vesalius showed where the ancient authority was wrong. It changed how anatomy was taught and set observation above textual authority.

It was not a solitary achievement: Vesalius built on a broader movement of anatomical study and on the skills of the artists and printers who made the book.

title: Fabrici describes the valves of the veins
summary: In 1603 Girolamo Fabrici (Fabricius ab Aquapendente), professor of anatomy at Padua, published De venarum ostiolis, the most detailed illustrated account of the valves in the veins to that date. He misread their purpose; his student William Harvey later used them as evidence that blood circulates.
explanation:
Valves inside the veins had been noticed by earlier anatomists, but Fabrici, professor of anatomy and surgery at Padua from 1565, examined them systematically. He demonstrated them in 1579 and in 1603 published a short illustrated treatise on them, De venarum ostiolis ('On the little doors of the veins'), printed in Padua.

He noted that the valves always point towards the heart. Following Galen, however, he believed that blood flowed outward through the veins, and explained the valves as brakes that stopped too much blood flowing back into the limbs, where the veins might burst.

William Harvey studied at Padua from 1598 to 1602, when Fabrici was at the height of his fame, and learned about the valves there. Harvey later explained them quite differently, as part of his theory of the circulation of the blood.

date.basis: Year De venarum ostiolis was published in Padua. Fabrici had demonstrated the valves in 1579 (some accounts say 1574).

people.name: Girolamo Fabrici (Hieronymus Fabricius ab Aquapendente)
people.role: Professor of anatomy and surgery, University of Padua

whatChanged: Gave anatomists a detailed, illustrated description of the venous valves and showed that they always face towards the heart.
whyItMattered: The valves became one of the pieces of evidence Harvey used to argue that blood returns to the heart and circulates.
limitations: Valves in the veins had been seen before Fabrici; his claim to have discovered them has been contested.
Fabrici's explanation of what the valves were for, based on Galen's physiology, was wrong.
contested: Sources give 1574 or 1579 for his first observation of the valves, and recent scholarship questions his claim to have discovered them.

sources.supports: Professor of anatomy and surgery at Padua from 1565; anatomy theatre opened 1594; demonstrated vein valves in 1579; priority recently contested; supervised William Harvey, who learned about the valves in Padua.

sources.citation: Edward Worth Library, Dublin. Teaching anatomy: Padua, sixteenth century.
sources.supports: De venarum ostiolis (Padua, 1603) included a detailed description of the valves in the veins.

title: Harvey shows that the blood circulates
summary: In 1628 William Harvey, physician at St Bartholomew's Hospital in London, published De motu cordis, arguing from experiment and measurement that the heart pumps a fixed volume of blood around the body in a circuit.
explanation:
Harvey had studied at Padua and was appointed physician to St Bartholomew's Hospital in London in 1609. He investigated the movement of the blood by observation and experiment, working mostly on dogs and on cold-blooded animals such as frogs and snakes, whose slower hearts were easier to watch.

His decisive argument was quantitative. The heart pushes out so much blood with each beat that the body could not possibly make that amount anew, so a fixed volume of blood must go round and round, driven by the heart acting as a pump. He was already saying this at the end of his Lumleian lectures at the College of Physicians in 1616, but he published only in 1628, in a short Latin book printed in Frankfurt, then a centre of the European book trade.

The book was fiercely attacked; one critic called the idea paradoxical, useless, false, impossible, absurd and harmful. Harvey could not see how blood passed from the arteries to the veins and had to suppose that there were hidden connections. Marcello Malpighi observed the capillaries in 1661.

date.basis: Year De motu cordis was published in Frankfurt. Harvey's notes for his 1616 Lumleian lecture show he had reached the conclusion by then.

locations.name: St Bartholomew's Hospital, London
locations.role: Where Harvey worked as physician while developing and teaching the theory

locations.name: Frankfurt am Main
locations.role: Where De motu cordis was printed in 1628

people.name: William Harvey
people.role: Physician to St Bartholomew's Hospital; Lumleian lecturer at the College of Physicians

whatChanged: Replaced the idea that blood is continually produced and used up with a circulation driven by the heart as a pump.
whyItMattered: Circulation became a foundation of physiology, and the book showed how experiment and measurement could overturn an ancient authority.
limitations: Harvey could not see the capillaries linking arteries and veins; Malpighi observed them in 1661.
Parts of the circuit, such as the passage of blood through the lungs, had been described earlier (see Ibn al-Nafis); Harvey's contribution was the whole circuit and its experimental proof.
His experiments relied on live animals, mostly dogs.

sources.supports: Calculation of how much blood the heart pumps per hour led Harvey to conclude that blood is circulated, not continually produced; publication delayed until 1628.

title: Hooke's Micrographia names the cell
summary: In 1665 Robert Hooke, curator of experiments to the Royal Society in London, published Micrographia, the first illustrated book of observations made with microscopes. Describing thin slices of cork, he called their tiny compartments 'cells'.
explanation:
Hooke built one of the best compound microscopes of his time, with its own lighting system, and used it in demonstrations at the Royal Society's weekly meetings, where he had been curator of experiments since 1662. Micrographia (1665) set out his observations with large engraved illustrations, including a famous flea, and became a best-seller.

In thin slices of cork he saw a honeycomb of small box-like spaces, which reminded him of the cells of a monastery, and he named them accordingly. What he saw were the walls of dead plant tissue. The word was later adopted for the basic unit of living things.

Antoni van Leeuwenhoek, who knew Hooke's work, built far more powerful microscopes and reported protozoa, bacteria, red blood cells and sperm cells in letters that the Royal Society translated and published.

people.name: Robert Hooke
people.role: Curator of Experiments, Royal Society of London

whatChanged: Showed in detail what a microscope could reveal and introduced the word 'cell' for a biological structure.
whyItMattered: Microscopy went on to reveal micro-organisms and blood cells, and the cell became the basic unit of biology and of medicine's understanding of disease.
limitations: Hooke saw empty cell walls in dead cork, not living cells.
Leeuwenhoek's more powerful microscopes, not Hooke's, first revealed bacteria and blood cells.

sources.citation: University of California Museum of Paleontology. Robert Hooke (1635–1703).
sources.supports: Micrographia published 1665, a best-seller; Hooke's compound microscope and illumination system used at Royal Society meetings; Curator of Experiments from 1662; cork observation and the name 'cells'.

sources.citation: Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford. Moments in Medicine: Micrographia, Robert Hooke, 1665.
sources.supports: First illustrated book of observations using microscopes; first use of 'cell' for biological organisms; Leeuwenhoek's microscopes revealed protozoa, bacteria, red blood cells and sperm cells, published by the Royal Society.

sources.citation: Pearce JMS. Robert Hooke and Micrographia. Hektoen International, Spring 2023.
sources.supports: Hooke was first to show the cell; devised one of the earliest microscopes; the cell underlies understanding of the unit of life.

title: Amyand removes a perforated appendix
summary: In 1735 at St George's Hospital, London, the surgeon Claudius Amyand operated on an 11-year-old boy's hernia and found inside it an appendix perforated by a swallowed pin. He removed it: the earliest recorded successful appendicectomy.
explanation:
Hanvil Anderson, aged 11, was admitted to St George's Hospital at Hyde Park Corner with a scrotal hernia he had had since infancy and a fistula between the scrotum and thigh. When Amyand, the hospital's principal surgeon, opened the hernia he found the appendix inside it, pierced by a pin encrusted with stone. He removed the pin and the damaged appendix, and the operation succeeded.

Amyand described the case in a paper read to the Royal Society on 11 December 1735 and published in its Philosophical Transactions. It was an unplanned response to what he found, not a treatment for appendicitis, and the case fell into obscurity. Removing the appendix became an established operation only in the 1880s, after anaesthesia and antisepsis had made abdominal surgery far safer.

An appendix lying within an inguinal hernia is still called Amyand's hernia.

date.basis: Several sources date the operation to 6 December 1735; Amyand's paper was read to the Royal Society on 11 December 1735. Wikipedia's timeline gives 1736.

locations.name: St George's Hospital, Hyde Park Corner, London
locations.modern: Hyde Park Corner, London, England, UK

people.name: Claudius Amyand
people.role: Principal Surgeon, St George's Hospital; Serjeant Surgeon to the King

people.name: Hanvil Anderson
people.role: The 11-year-old patient

whatChanged: Recorded, for the first time, the successful surgical removal of the appendix.
whyItMattered: It showed that the appendix could be removed and the patient survive, although the operation did not become routine for another 150 years.
limitations: 'Earliest recorded' means the earliest known written report; earlier, unrecorded operations cannot be ruled out.
Amyand was repairing a hernia and removed the appendix because of what he found; this was not a planned operation for appendicitis.
The case had little influence at the time; appendicectomy was established independently in the 1880s.

title: Priestley isolates oxygen at Bowood
summary: On 1 August 1774, in the Earl of Shelburne's laboratory at Bowood House in Wiltshire, Joseph Priestley heated red mercuric oxide and collected a new gas. He called it 'dephlogisticated air'; Lavoisier named it oxygen.
explanation:
Priestley, a dissenting minister and teacher, investigated gases ('airs') from the early 1770s and described several new ones, among them nitrous oxide. In 1773 he became librarian and companion to the Earl of Shelburne, whose estate at Bowood gave him a laboratory. There, on 1 August 1774, he heated red mercuric oxide and isolated a new air.

He interpreted it through the then-dominant phlogiston theory of burning and called it 'dephlogisticated air'. Later that year, in Paris, he told Antoine Lavoisier about it. Lavoisier recognised it as part of the atmosphere, named it oxygen and used it to overturn the phlogiston theory. Priestley never accepted the new chemistry.

The Swedish apothecary Carl Wilhelm Scheele prepared the same gas, probably earlier, but published later.

date.basis: Date of the experiment at Bowood, as given by the Science History Institute, the Bowood estate and the American Chemical Society. Priestley announced the discovery in a letter read to the Royal Society in 1775.

people.name: Joseph Priestley
people.role: Natural philosopher and dissenting minister; librarian to the Earl of Shelburne

people.name: William Petty, 2nd Earl of Shelburne
people.role: Patron who provided the laboratory at Bowood

whatChanged: Isolated the gas that Lavoisier identified as a component of air and named oxygen.
whyItMattered: Oxygen was central to the new chemistry of burning and, in time, to the understanding of how the body uses the air it breathes.
limitations: Priestley did not understand his gas as a new element; Lavoisier did.
This is a discovery in chemistry; its medical importance came later and indirectly.
contested: Priority is disputed: Scheele prepared oxygen, probably by 1772, but published after Priestley, and Lavoisier's own claims to independent discovery have been questioned.

sources.citation: Science History Institute. Joseph Priestley (historical profile).
sources.supports: Isolated a new air on 1 August 1774; called it dephlogisticated air under phlogiston theory; demonstrated it to Lavoisier, who named it oxygen and campaigned against phlogiston; Priestley resisted the new chemistry.

sources.citation: Bowood House and Gardens. World Book Day: Joseph Priestley.
sources.supports: Oxygen discovered in the laboratory at Bowood on 1 August 1774; Priestley employed by Lord Shelburne from 1773 as librarian; gases isolated during his seven years there.

title: Withering's account of the foxglove
summary: In 1785 William Withering, physician to the General Hospital in Birmingham, published An Account of the Foxglove: 163 patients with dropsy treated with foxglove leaf, reported whether they did well or not, with a clear description of the drug's dangerous side effects.
explanation:
Foxglove had been known to herbalists for centuries. Withering, who joined the staff of Birmingham's General Hospital in 1775, was asked about a family remedy for dropsy kept secret by an old woman in Shropshire. The mixture contained at least twenty herbs, and he concluded that the active one could be no other than the foxglove.

Over about ten years he tried different preparations, found dried, powdered leaf more reliable than fresh leaf or a decoction, and learned to adjust the dose. His book reports 163 cases. He chose to include every patient he had treated, whether the outcome was good or bad, because a selection of successes would have misled his readers. He described the toxic effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and disturbed, green-yellow vision) and advised stopping and restarting at a lower dose when they appeared.

He did not know how foxglove worked. He thought mainly of its effect on urine, though he noticed that it could calm a disordered heartbeat. Other physicians later used it in excessive doses or where it could not help.

date.basis: Year the book was printed in Birmingham. The cases it reports were collected between 1775 and 1784.

people.name: William Withering
people.role: Physician to the General Hospital, Birmingham

people.name: An unnamed woman in Shropshire
people.role: Kept a family remedy for dropsy that contained foxglove

whatChanged: Turned a folk remedy into a medicine with a described preparation, dose, effects and dangers, based on a systematic record of patients.
whyItMattered: Digitalis became a landmark treatment for heart failure for well over a century, and the book is an early example of reporting every treated case, not just the successes.
limitations: Withering did not understand how the drug acted and could not reliably say which patients would benefit.
The Shropshire woman is known only from Withering's brief mention; her name and knowledge were not recorded.
Problems of dosing and toxicity were not resolved for about a century.

sources.citation: Withering W. An Account of the Foxglove, and Some of Its Medical Uses: with Practical Remarks on Dropsy, and Other Diseases. Birmingham: M. Swinney; 1785 (Project Gutenberg edition).
sources.supports: Physician to the General Hospital at Birmingham; printed in Birmingham in 1785; about ten years' use; every case mentioned, proper or improper, successful or not.

sources.citation: Lee MR. William Withering (1741–1799): a biographical sketch of a Birmingham Lunatic. James Lind Library, 2005.
sources.supports: Joined Birmingham General Hospital in 1775; Shropshire wise woman's remedy of at least 20 herbs, active herb the foxglove; dried leaf more effective; 163 patients; side effects including green/yellow vision; uncertain mechanism; later misuse.

sources.citation: Hektoen International. William Withering and the foxglove (2017).
sources.supports: 1785 book on ten years of use; in 1775 asked about a remedy kept secret by an old woman in Shropshire; studied at Birmingham General Hospital; a milestone in treating heart failure.

sources.citation: University of Iowa, John Martin Rare Book Room (HEIRS). Withering W. An account of the foxglove (1785).
sources.supports: Book includes 163 cases; digitalis in the Edinburgh pharmacopoeia in 1783 and later overuse; regarded as a classic of pharmacology.

title: Hahnemann founds homeopathy
summary: In 1796 the German physician Samuel Hahnemann published the principle that 'like cures like', drawn from taking cinchona bark himself in 1790. Homeopathy spread widely in the nineteenth century; reviews of the evidence have found no health condition for which it reliably works.
explanation:
Hahnemann was critical of the medicine of his day. In 1790, living near Leipzig and translating the Scottish physician William Cullen's Materia Medica, he rejected Cullen's explanation of why cinchona bark helped against malarial fevers and took the bark himself for several days. He reported symptoms resembling the fever, and concluded that a substance which causes symptoms in a healthy person can cure similar symptoms in someone who is ill.

He first published this 'principle of similars' in 1796, in a German journal of practical medicine, and in 1810 set out his system in the Organon. Homeopathic remedies came to be given in extremely diluted forms. By the late nineteenth century homeopathy was practised in more than 30 countries, with its own medical schools and hospitals, and it remains popular in parts of Europe and in India.

Its principles have not stood up to testing. In 2015 Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council concluded, after assessing the published systematic reviews, that there are no health conditions for which there is reliable evidence that homeopathy is effective.

date.basis: Year Hahnemann first published the principle of similars. His self-experiment with cinchona dates from 1790; Wikipedia's timeline gives 1790.

locations.name: Stötteritz, near Leipzig, Electorate of Saxony
locations.role: Where Hahnemann translated Cullen and tested cinchona on himself (1790)

people.name: Samuel Hahnemann
people.role: Physician, chemist and translator; founder of homeopathy

whatChanged: Founded a system of treatment based on 'like cures like' and highly diluted remedies, which became a widespread alternative to orthodox medicine.
whyItMattered: Homeopathy became one of the most popular alternative therapies in the world, which makes its lack of demonstrated effect a continuing public-health issue.
limitations: Hahnemann's conclusion rested on his own reaction to cinchona; controlled tests of homeopathic remedies have not supported it.
This entry is included because it shaped medical history, not because the method works.
contested: Supporters of homeopathy, including the Homeopathy Research Institute, dispute the methods of the 2015 Australian review, arguing that its definition of reliable evidence was too strict. The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners maintains that the claim of effectiveness is not supported by systematic reviews.
harms: The Australian review warned that people who choose homeopathy may put their health at risk if they reject or delay treatments for which there is good evidence of safety and effectiveness.

title: Davy suggests nitrous oxide against surgical pain
summary: Experimenting at the Medical Pneumatic Institution in Bristol, the young chemist Humphry Davy inhaled nitrous oxide repeatedly and in 1800 noted that, as it seemed capable of destroying physical pain, it might be used during surgical operations. The idea lay unused for over 40 years.
explanation:
The physician Thomas Beddoes opened the Pneumatic Institution at Clifton, Bristol, in 1798 to treat diseases such as consumption with inhaled gases, and hired Davy, then 19, to run its research. Rejecting the belief that nitrous oxide was deadly to breathe, Davy inhaled it many times, recording its effects on himself and on friends.

In 1800 he published a 580-page account of the work. Near the end, almost in passing, he remarked that because nitrous oxide appeared capable of destroying physical pain, it might probably be used with advantage during surgical operations in which there was little bleeding.

Nobody followed this up. The gas became known as laughing gas, and its use against surgical pain was not pursued until the 1840s. In January 1845 the dentist Horace Wells tried to demonstrate it at Massachusetts General Hospital; the patient groaned and moved, and the demonstration was judged a failure.

date.basis: Year Davy's Researches, Chemical and Philosophical; Chiefly Concerning Nitrous Oxide was published. The experiments took place in 1799; Wikipedia's timeline lists both years.

people.name: Humphry Davy
people.role: Superintendent of the Medical Pneumatic Institution

people.name: Thomas Beddoes
people.role: Physician who founded the Institution

whatChanged: Showed that nitrous oxide could be breathed safely and recorded that it relieved pain.
whyItMattered: Nitrous oxide later became one of the first anaesthetic gases; the long gap before anyone acted on Davy's remark shows that an observation alone does not change practice.
limitations: Davy's remark was a passing comment, and historians differ on how much he was concerned with surgical pain.
Nitrous oxide on its own gives a lighter state of unconsciousness than ether, which helps explain Wells's failure in 1845.

title: Desault's clinical school and surgical journal
summary: At the Hôtel-Dieu in Paris, the surgeon Pierre-Joseph Desault built a clinical school that taught surgery at the bedside, in French, to students from across Europe. In 1791 he founded the Journal de chirurgie to record the most instructive cases from his wards.
explanation:
Desault, born in Franche-Comté and trained partly in a military hospital, opened a school of anatomy in Paris in 1766 that drew around 300 pupils, to the resentment of established teachers. After posts at the Charité hospital, he took charge of surgery at the Hôtel-Dieu, Paris's main public hospital, in the mid-1780s.

There he organised teaching around patients: students followed cases on the wards and watched and practised procedures, with lectures given in French rather than Latin. In 1791 he founded the Journal de chirurgie, edited by his pupils, which published the most interesting cases from his clinical school together with his comments on them.

His students, among them Xavier Bichat, spread his methods; much of what is known of his teaching comes from their publications after his death in 1795.

date.basis: Year the Journal de chirurgie was established. Desault's clinical school at the Hôtel-Dieu dates from the late 1780s.

locations.name: Hôtel-Dieu, Paris
locations.modern: Île de la Cité, Paris, France

people.name: Pierre-Joseph Desault

whyItMattered: Bedside clinical teaching and case reporting became the model for the Paris school of medicine and spread internationally.
